title: The month of Bhadon
hookLine: in Bhadon she is lost in doubt, attached to what is second (Barah Maha, ang 134)

cards: The rain has stopped being a relief. Clothes won't dry. Mosquitoes are everywhere.
This is Bhadon, roughly August into September, the sticky end of the monsoon. The air is so thick it's hard to think, and the paths that were clear in spring are overgrown and muddy.
It's easy to lose your way in a field in Bhadon. Guru Arjan says the soul can lose its way too, in a fog a lot like that weather, and he has a word for it.

teach.b: The word is bharam. The Bhadon stanza on ang 134 opens, in paraphrase: in Bhadon, she has lost her way in bharam, attached to the second. Bharam is often translated doubt, but that can mislead.
In Gurbani it isn't the honest question a curious person asks. It's closer to delusion, a mind going round in circles in the fog.
And doojaa, the second, is Gurbani's word for duality: loving something else in place of the One. Then the stanza gets hard.

She may adorn herself a hundred thousand ways; it accomplishes nothing. On the day the body perishes, people will speak of it as a ghost. Death's messengers seize her and lead her away, and tell no one their secret.
Those she was attached to every day leave her standing in a moment. She wrings her hands; her body writhes; the black hair has turned white. As she sows, so she reaps: karma is the field.
It's a vivid, uncomfortable picture, and meant to be: a life spent in the fog, decorated outside, lost inside, waking only when it's too late to plant anything new. But the stanza doesn't end there.

teach.h: THE BOAT OF THE ONE'S FEET.
teach.b: Nanak seeks the One's sanctuary, it says, and the One gives the boat of His feet.
Those protected by the Guru aren't thrown into hell in Bhadon. So the fog has an exit: not thinking harder, not more adornment, but taking refuge.
The boat is the same image as the Guru's boat in the Asa di Var: what carries you across when you can't find the path on foot.

how: On the sangrand of Bhadon, gurdwaras that keep the day read the Bhadon stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, with its warning against bharam and its promise of the One's sanctuary.

o: a festival that marks the end of the rains
a boat that carries pilgrims across a river
the heavy late-monsoon month, lost in fog

games.q: the month of Bhadon — tap the pairs.
p: given to the one who seeks refuge

s: in Gurbani, bharam means asking honest questions
it's closer to delusion: a mind wandering in circles in the fog.
the Bhadon stanza says as she sows, so she reaps
the stanza ends with no way out of the fog
the One gives the boat of His feet to the one who seeks sanctuary.

games.q: you're lost in the fog of Bhadon, adorned on the outside, circling on the inside. what does the stanza say carries you out?
o: taking refuge; the One gives the boat of His feet.
games.why: Nanak seeks the One's sanctuary, and the One gives the boat of His feet. those protected by the Guru aren't cast away.

practice: Honest questions are welcome; this is about a fog.
Find one place where your mind keeps circling without getting anywhere, a worry you replay, a choice you keep avoiding, and name it plainly in one sentence, since naming it can thin the fog a little.
Then picture stepping into a boat that carries you across without having to figure it all out first, and if you pray, say Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Bhadon. The heavy end of the rains, when the soul is lost in bharam, attached to the second, until it takes refuge in the boat of the One's feet.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: in bharam, delusion or wandering; the stanza's opening sound echoes Bhadon.

carryVoice: Your line: bhadon: doubt. The way out of the fog is refuge, not more effort. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Barah Maha, Majh M5, Bhadon stanza, Ang 134
